name: Faith healing

lead: Faith healing is the practice of seeking recovery or relief through prayer, ritual and the laying on of hands, usually within a religious tradition. Practitioners and participants describe benefits for pain, stress, mood and a sense of wholeness.

In appearance terms the link is indirect: people who feel calmer, less anxious and more hopeful often report better sleep, mood and self-presentation, and some use faith-based practice for skin, hair or body concerns alongside other care. Research has studied prayer and religious healing mostly for mental health, pain and spiritual distress, with mixed results.

paras: Practice ranges from personal prayer to healing services, prayer camps, pilgrimages such as Lourdes, priesthood blessings and visits to individual healers. Many users combine it with conventional medical treatment, and qualitative studies report that people often value it most in that combination.

The main documented harm is delay or refusal of effective medical treatment. The American Cancer Society and the American Medical Association advise that prayer should not replace or postpone conventional care, and court cases involving children who died after medical care was withheld are well documented. Fraud by some televangelist healers has also been exposed.

Lower perceived stress and greater sense of hope
Better mood and sleep, steadier confidence in appearance and bearing
angle.text: People who practise faith healing describe feeling calmer and more hopeful, which they associate with better sleep, mood and self-presentation. Some turn to it for skin, hair or body concerns alongside other care. This is a wellbeing pathway rather than a direct physical effect on appearance.

lead: Faith healing is the use of prayer, ritual gestures such as the laying on of hands, and trust in divine or spiritual power to promote recovery from illness or distress. It is most closely associated with Christianity, especially Pentecostal and Charismatic churches, but comparable practices exist in Catholic, Latter-day Saint, Islamic, Buddhist and many traditional healing contexts.[1][2]

For people interested in how they look and feel, faith healing is relevant mainly through wellbeing: proponents describe reduced stress and anxiety, steadier mood and renewed hope, and psychologists have proposed behavioural, interpersonal, cognitive, affective and psychophysiological pathways by which faith might support health.[3] Calmer, better-rested people commonly carry themselves with more confidence, which is the chain through which the practice touches appearance.

Research includes a Cochrane review of intercessory prayer that did not find a positive effect in most studies, a randomised trial of combining psychiatric care with prayer-camp healing in Ghana, and qualitative reviews reporting that users perceive traditional and faith healing as helpful, especially alongside biomedical treatment.[1][4][5]

paras: Faith healing covers a range of practices in which prayer, blessing or ritual is believed to bring physical or spiritual healing. Common forms include laying on of hands, anointing with oil, healing services, group prayer and visits to healers or shrines.[1][2]

Traditions differ on the role of the patient's own belief. Christian Scientists, for example, rely on prayer but do not describe themselves as faith healers, because they say healing does not depend on the patient's faith.[1] The Catholic Church recognises both medical healing and healing through divine grace, and the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith issued guidance on healing prayers in 2000.[1]

Healing through religious ritual is ancient. In Greece, patients slept in temples of Asclepius after purification and received treatment suggested in dreams, and Egyptian medicine combined faith healing with surgery and embalming practices.[1][6] Cures have been reported at Lourdes since 1858.[1]

The modern Pentecostal movement began in the early twentieth century under Charles Fox Parham, and the 1906 Azusa Street Revival in Los Angeles led by William J. Seymour brought it international attention.[1] After the Second World War, William Branham and Oral Roberts led healing revivals, followed by Kathryn Kuhlman, Jack Coe, A. A. Allen and later televangelists such as Benny Hinn.[1] Magician James Randi documented the fraud of healer Peter Popoff in a book on faith healers.[1]

Proponents hold that faith, prayer and divine intervention can contribute to healing of body and mind. A psychological review defined faith as a congruence of belief, trust and obedience and proposed five hypothesised mechanisms linking faith and health: behavioural, interpersonal, cognitive, affective and psychophysiological.[3]
A neuroscience review of salutogenic mechanisms noted that beliefs need not be realistic to benefit health, citing faith healing and the placebo effect as examples of outlook affecting wellbeing.[7]

Surveys of hospital inpatients have found that many patients hold positive attitudes toward discussing religious belief with their physicians.[8] In many low- and middle-income countries, faith and traditional healers are a common first or parallel source of care for mental health, HIV and chronic conditions, and reviews describe patients moving between healers and clinics.[4][9]

A randomised trial in a Ghana prayer camp assigned residents with serious mental illness to psychiatric medication plus usual prayer-camp care or to usual prayer-camp care alone, to evaluate combining the two approaches ethically.[10] A randomised trial in breast cancer patients examined intercessory prayer on spiritual distress, anxiety, depression and salivary amylase during radiotherapy.[11] A trial of belief in psychic healing examined self-reported pain in people with chronic pain.[12]

A systematic review of sixteen qualitative studies found that users perceived traditional and faith healing as effective for mental illness, particularly when combined with biomedical treatment.[4] A Cochrane review of intercessory prayer reported that most studies did not show a positive effect, and its authors did not consider further trials warranted.[1]

The American Cancer Society states that evidence does not support claims that faith healing cures physical ailments, and cites a 1998 review of 172 child deaths in which conventional treatment would likely have given most children a survival rate above 90 percent.[1] The American Medical Association has stated that prayer as therapy should not delay conventional medical care.[1]

In the United States, 31 states have religious exemptions in child neglect laws, and several parents have been convicted of manslaughter or reckless homicide after withholding care, including cases in Wisconsin (2009) and Oregon (2014 and 2017).[1] Reports also describe people who stopped HIV medication after being told they were cured.[1]

timeline.event: Cures begin to be reported at Lourdes.[1]
Azusa Street Revival in Los Angeles spreads Pentecostal healing worldwide.[1]
Healing revivals led by William Branham and Oral Roberts; tent crusades follow.[1]
CAPTA requires states to offer religious exemptions in child neglect laws to receive federal funds.[1]
Vatican guidance on healing prayers issued.[1]
